title: Add maintenance-mode API behavior + write-path blocking during restore (Private)
creator: Rafael Mendes
description:
Problem
During in-place restores for Redwood Private, operators need a safe way to prevent additional writes while control-plane state (DB, config/policy, integrations metadata) is being rewound. Today, restores rely on best-effort operator coordination ("stop traffic") and partial service stoppage, which is error-prone and makes RTO unpredictable.

Goal
Introduce a first-class "maintenance mode" that can be toggled by the restore toolchain to:
- Block write paths (and optionally other non-essential endpoints) with clear, operator-actionable errors.
- Provide machine-readable status so the installer/restore jobs can gate progress.
- Remain backwards compatible with older clients/operators during rolling upgrades.

Scope
- Control plane API behavior changes: rejecting writes when maintenance mode is enabled.
- A single source of truth for maintenance mode state (persisted) and emitted events/metrics.
- Integration tests for write rejection + messaging.
- Backwards compatibility notes (what breaks, what’s preserved, upgrade order).

Non-goals
- Traffic management / ingress-level WAF rules (operators may still choose to restrict ingress, but not required).
- Blocking all reads (reads should remain available unless explicitly unsafe).

Proposed behavior
1) Maintenance mode state
- New persisted flag: control-plane "maintenance_mode" boolean + optional reason string and "set_by" (tooling).
- Must survive restarts (stored in control-plane DB) so behavior is consistent across pod reschedules.

2) API request handling
- Write endpoints (mutations) return HTTP 503 Service Unavailable while maintenance mode is enabled.
- Response body must include:
  - stable error code: RW_MAINTENANCE_MODE
  - message: "Cluster is in maintenance mode (restore in progress). Retry later or follow restore runbook."
  - optional "reason" if set (e.g., "restore-in-place")
  - Retry-After header: 30 (seconds) to encourage clients to back off
- Reads remain served. Exception: endpoints that implicitly mutate (e.g., “create token”, “rotate cert”, “apply policy”) must be treated as writes.

3) Tooling / operator UX
- Restore pipeline will:
  - enable maintenance mode before DB restore / PITR
  - verify maintenance mode is effective (health check that a representative write is rejected)
  - disable maintenance mode only after restore validation gates pass
- If restore fails mid-flight, restore job should keep maintenance mode enabled and instruct operator to either retry restore or execute rollback plan.

Backwards compatibility / upgrade notes
- Rolling upgrades:
  - Older control-plane components that do not understand maintenance mode must not crash if the flag exists; they simply won’t enforce write blocking.
  - Therefore, upgrade order recommendation: upgrade control plane components first (to versions that enforce maintenance mode), then rely on restore tooling.
- Clients:
  - Existing clients may not parse structured error code; must still see a clear human-readable message.
  - Using 503 (not 401/403) avoids implying auth problems and encourages retry/backoff semantics.

Acceptance criteria
- When maintenance mode is enabled, all defined write routes return 503 + RW_MAINTENANCE_MODE + Retry-After.
- At least one integration test verifies:
  - a normal write succeeds when maintenance mode is disabled
  - the same write fails with expected status/body when enabled
- Installer/restore tooling can toggle maintenance mode and verify enforcement (restore precheck step).
- Docs snippet added to restore runbooks: expected error, what it means, when it’s safe to disable.

Testing plan
- Unit tests: route-level guard / middleware behavior.
- Integration tests: maintenance mode toggling + write rejection.
- Manual: run in a staging Private cluster; enable maintenance mode and confirm:
  - writes rejected
  - reads still work
  - dashboards/metrics show state transition

Observability
- Emit structured event on enable/disable with actor + reason.
- Metric: maintenance_mode_state (gauge) + maintenance_mode_transitions_total.

Notes / risks
- Need careful audit for "write-like" endpoints that are not obvious (token issuance, cert rotation, connector config updates).
- Ensure error responses don’t leak sensitive internal state; keep message generic and runbook-driven.
comments: 2025-10-29 (Miles Thornton): Strongly prefer persistence in DB vs ConfigMap so the behavior survives restarts during restore. Also recommend 503 + Retry-After to avoid clients hammering the API during restore.

2025-10-30 (Sean Gallagher): Please make the rejection error actionable: include a stable code + plain-language message. SRE wants to link this in the on-call checklist and have the installer validate enforcement before proceeding.

2025-11-01 (Diego Santos): Watch for endpoints that mutate indirectly (e.g., "refresh" operations that write caches). We should explicitly tag routes as read/write in the router and gate writes centrally.
2025-11-04 (Vivek Kulkarni): Back-compat is key: older operators must not get stuck. Document upgrade order: control plane first, then restore tooling usage.
2025-11-08 (Allison Grant): Add a gauge metric for maintenance mode so dashboards can annotate restore drills and we can alert if a cluster stays in maintenance mode > N hours.

resolution: Implemented maintenance-mode enforcement in control plane: write routes return 503 + RW_MAINTENANCE_MODE + Retry-After, with integration test coverage. Restore tooling toggles maintenance mode as part of restore sequencing. Added notes for rolling upgrade order and operator-facing messaging.
